newsitem.title: UK: UK building societies relish resurgence prospect.
newsitem.headline: UK building societies relish resurgence prospect.

text.p: Britain's building societies are staging a resurgence after the uncertainties raised by changes in the sector over the last year, the head of the largest mutually-owned society said on Wednesday.

Brian Davis, chief executive of Nationwide Building Society and chairman of the Building Societies Association (BSA), told the trade body's annual meeting that savers were flocking to take up the rates offered by building societies.
The Nationwide will be confirmed as the largest building society when Halifax Building Society becomes a publicly listed company at the beginning of June.
"Societies' savings are increasing as the combination of being seen as both a prudent investment and as a good punt for speculators come together to provide the obvious home for savers," Davis said.

Building societies, the traditional lenders to Britain's homeowners, have been trumpeting the benefits of their mutual status after some of the biggest societies opted to leave this behind in favour of becoming publicly-quoted banks.

Davis said mortgage business continued to flow to the societies, dismissing suggestions that the housing market in Britain -- which has seen significant rises in certain areas over the last 12 months -- was overheating.

But he also warned the new Labour government, which has pledged not to increase personal taxes, that it should not "introduce a tax by the back door" by imposing restrictions the tax relief on mortgage interest, known as MIRAS.

"The cloud of potential MIRAS resrictions has not yet impacted and perhaps the government will recognise the foolishness of trying to introduce a tax by the back door - especially as it will obviously penalise the poorer mortgage customers the most," Davis said.

Delegates to the BSA annual conference also heard from the Building Societies Commission (BSC) chairman Geoffrey Fitchew that there would be no immediate change to the way they were regulated following the financial regulatory shake-up announced by Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Tuesday.
The BSC was set up under the Building Societies Act of 1986 as the regulator and supervisor of the sector.

"No decision has been taken at this stage to change the present arrangements," Fitchew said. And the views of the BSA and the building societies would be given "particular attention" in deciding any changes, he added.

The new Labour government said it would form a new statutory "super-regulator" for Britain's financial sector, wrapping together the existing self-regulatory organisations which were created by the Financial Services Act of 1986.

Building societies will not immediately fall under the auspices of the revamped Securities and Investment Board (SIB), although some building society delegates said it would be a good thing for them in the long run if they did, as it would given them the opportunity to widen the scope of services they offer.

Fitchew had words of encouragement for the 72 building societies represented by the BSA, telling them that they could "still put pressure on all retail finance institutions and produce better rates both for borrowers and savers".
"A strong building society sector benefits every saver and borrower in the market, by keeping retail banks on their toes," Fitchew added.
